Summary: Trace a customer login end to end
Description:
*Business context*
You are new on the team and every support question starts with 'can the customer log in?'.

*Problem statement*
You do not yet know which classes, tables and log lines are involved when a customer signs in.

*Expected behaviour*
A written trace of POST /api/v1/auth/login from the browser to the database and back.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Names every class/method touched, in order
* Lists every table read or written and the columns that matter
* Shows the log lines of one login (with correlation id) and explains each
* Explains what happens on the 5th wrong password

*Scope*
Read-only. No code or data changes.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Map every screen of the customer app to its API calls
Description:
*Business context*
Support and QA need to know which backend call powers which screen.

*Problem statement*
There is no list of which endpoints each React screen calls.

*Expected behaviour*
A table: screen/route -> HTTP method + path -> request fields -> response fields used.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Covers all 9 customer routes
* Built from the browser Network tab, not guessed
* Notes any screen that calls more than one endpoint or the same endpoint twice

*Scope*
Read-only. Browser devtools + frontend/src/customer.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Explain how a payment is tied to what was bought
Description:
*Business context*
Finance asks 'what did payment 52913 pay for?' many times a week.

*Problem statement*
The payment table is shared by recharges, bookings and subscriptions and you cannot yet say how.

*Expected behaviour*
A short explanation plus three SQL queries that, given a payment id, return the thing that was bought for each kind.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Explains the rule the database enforces
* Queries run against the large dataset and return rows
* Mentions what happens when someone tries to break the rule

*Scope*
Read-only SQL.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Find where each role and permission is enforced
Description:
*Business context*
A reviewer asked 'can a support agent see another customer's tickets?' and nobody could answer quickly.

*Problem statement*
Authorization is spread over security configuration, controller annotations and service checks.

*Expected behaviour*
A matrix: endpoint group x role (CUSTOMER / SUPPORT_AGENT / ADMIN) with the exact permission codes required and the file/line that enforces it.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Covers admin, support, payment, customer and public endpoints
* Cites file and line for each rule
* Lists at least two places where the rule is checked in more than one layer

*Scope*
Read-only.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Trace a recharge from click to rows
Description:
*Business context*
Recharges are the highest-volume operation and the most common source of tickets.

*Problem statement*
You do not know which rows are created when a customer starts a recharge, in which order, and in which transaction.

*Expected behaviour*
A trace of POST /recharges: the SQL statements, the rows created, the status of each, and what is rolled back if a later step fails.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Lists each INSERT/UPDATE/SELECT FOR UPDATE with the table
* States the initial status of every created row
* Describes the effect of retrying with the same idempotency key
* Includes the correlation-id log lines

*Scope*
Read-only; use the dev database.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Trace a payment callback (confirm) and its side effects
Description:
*Business context*
Payment confirmation changes several tables; support needs to predict the outcome.

*Problem statement*
It is unclear what changes when a payment is confirmed as SUCCEEDED versus FAILED, and what a repeated callback does.

*Expected behaviour*
A before/after table of every row changed by confirm SUCCEEDED and FAILED for a recharge, a booking and a subscription payment.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Covers all three payment parents
* States what a repeated callback with the same id does
* States what a different outcome with the same callback id does
* Lists the notifications created

*Scope*
Read-only; run the calls yourself and diff the rows.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Trace how a seat is claimed and released
Description:
*Business context*
'Seat already taken' complaints need a precise explanation.

*Problem statement*
You cannot yet say which row represents a taken seat or when it disappears.

*Expected behaviour*
A description of the lifecycle of a seat: when it is taken, which events release it, and what the availability endpoint reports at each step.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Identifies the table and key that represent a taken seat
* Covers payment failure, cancellation, expiry and refund
* Demonstrated with real calls against one catalogue item

*Scope*
Read-only plus normal use of the API.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Follow one request through the logs using its correlation id
Description:
*Business context*
Every production investigation begins with a correlation id.

*Problem statement*
You have not yet used the correlation id to connect a UI error, an API log line and an audit row.

*Expected behaviour*
Pick an admin action in the UI, then find: the response header, the access log line, the audit_event row, and the log line of any business event.

*Acceptance criteria*
* All four artefacts are found by the same id
* Explains where the id is created and where it is cleared
* Notes what is deliberately NOT logged

*Scope*
Read-only.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Read the Flyway history and explain V2 and V3
Description:
*Business context*
New engineers are warned never to edit old migrations.

*Problem statement*
Two migrations are empty files and nobody has explained why that is safe.

*Expected behaviour*
An explanation of flyway_schema_history, the checksum rule, and what would happen if V4 were edited or V2 deleted.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Shows the history table output
* Predicts the exact failure on edit/delete and then proves it on a scratch database (not connectone_dev)
* States the correct way to change a column today

*Scope*
Scratch database only (create a throwaway DB in the ConnectOne container, then drop it).

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Draw the payment and refund state machine from code and data
Description:
*Business context*
Support constantly asks 'what can happen next to this payment?'.

*Problem statement*
The allowed statuses are in the schema but the transitions are scattered through services.

*Expected behaviour*
A diagram of payment, recharge, booking and subscription statuses with the code path that moves each transition.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Every status value in the CHECK constraints appears
* Each arrow cites the method that causes it
* Marks any status that no code path ever produces, and any transition the data shows that no code path produces

*Scope*
Read-only.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Inventory every scheduled job and what it changes
Description:
*Business context*
Background jobs change data without an API call; on-call must know them.

*Problem statement*
There is no list of scheduled tasks, their frequency or their side effects.

*Expected behaviour*
A table of every @Scheduled method: schedule, tables touched, batch size, what happens if two instances run.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Complete (found by searching the code, not memory)
* States whether each job is safe to run on two instances at once
* Lists the property that changes each schedule

*Scope*
Read-only.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Profile the large dataset
Description:
*Business context*
You will spend weeks working against this data.

*Problem statement*
You do not yet know its size, shape or the controlled anomalies it contains.

*Expected behaviour*
A one-page profile: row counts, status distributions per table, busiest customers, date ranges, and the list of deliberate anomaly scenarios you can find with SQL.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Row counts match scripts/dataset verification output
* Includes at least 8 distinct anomaly queries with counts
* States which numbers change when the dataset is regenerated and which do not

*Scope*
Read-only SQL.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Find dead and unused code
Description:
*Business context*
A clean codebase is easier to change.

*Problem statement*
Some files look unused or empty.

*Expected behaviour*
A list of unused files/classes/properties with evidence (no references, zero bytes, unreferenced config) and a recommendation for each.

*Acceptance criteria*
* At least three findings with evidence
* Distinguishes 'safe to delete' from 'looks dead but is referenced indirectly'
* No deletions made (proposal only)

*Scope*
Read-only.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Explore logs, health and metrics
Description:
*Business context*
On-call needs to know what the running system will tell them.

*Problem statement*
You have not yet seen the health groups, metrics and log formats.

*Expected behaviour*
A cheat-sheet of: health/liveness/readiness URLs and what each reports for admin vs anonymous; five useful metric names; how to switch to JSON logs; how to raise one logger to DEBUG at runtime.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Every item demonstrated on the running system
* Includes the business counters created by payments
* Notes what anonymous callers can and cannot see

*Scope*
Read-only plus runtime logger change on your own instance.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Customers report being charged twice for one recharge
Description:
*Business context*
Support has received several 'charged twice' complaints this week. Each double charge is a refund and a bad review.

*Problem statement*
Some recharges show more than one successful payment row. Nobody knows how many customers or how much money is involved.

*Expected behaviour*
An incident note listing every affected recharge/customer, the money charged twice, the timing pattern, and a safe remediation plan (no data changed).

*Acceptance criteria*
* Complete list with counts and total amount
* Evidence that the extra payments are genuinely duplicates (timestamps, attempt numbers, keys)
* Proposed refund list that cannot over-refund
* Hypotheses for how it could happen, ranked, with what evidence would confirm each

*Scope*
Investigation and recommendation only. Do not change data.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: 'I paid but my recharge is pending/failed'
Description:
*Business context*
Customers say they were charged but did not get validity.

*Problem statement*
Some recharge rows and their payments disagree about the outcome.

*Expected behaviour*
A report of all recharge/payment disagreements, classified by type, with a recommended action per type.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Every disagreement type found and counted
* For each type: who is out of pocket (customer or company)
* Says which can be auto-fixed and which need a human
* Evidence queries included

*Scope*
Investigation only.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Payments stuck in PROCESSING although the provider called back
Description:
*Business context*
Ops has a growing pile of payments that never completed although the gateway says success.

*Problem statement*
Some payments are flagged for reconciliation and sit for days.

*Expected behaviour*
Quantify the backlog by age and amount, show the callback evidence for each, and write the runbook an on-call engineer would follow to clear it safely.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Backlog sized by age buckets and money
* Runbook uses the existing admin reconciliation screen/API
* Identifies which recharges are still waiting for these payments
* Lists risks of resolving in bulk

*Scope*
Investigation and runbook. Optionally resolve three payments through the UI to validate the runbook.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Customer 7777 produced hundreds of recharges in one day
Description:
*Business context*
Fraud monitoring flagged an unusual volume.

*Problem statement*
One customer has far more recharges in a single day than any other.

*Expected behaviour*
Determine whether it is abuse, a client bug or test traffic, using timing, plans, statuses, payments and numbers used; recommend controls.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Facts established with queries (counts per hour, plan mix, success rate, numbers used)
* A clear conclusion with confidence level and what would change it
* At least two preventive controls proposed (rate limit, velocity rule, alert)

*Scope*
Investigation only.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Support tickets stuck IN_PROGRESS for weeks
Description:
*Business context*
The support manager wants the stale queue cleaned up.

*Problem statement*
Many tickets are IN_PROGRESS with no recent activity; some urgent ones have no owner.

*Expected behaviour*
A report: stale tickets by agent and age, unowned urgent tickets, and tickets whose customer also has a failed payment.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Ages bucketed 14/30/60/90+ days
* Per-agent load table
* Unowned urgent list
* Recommendation for triage order

*Scope*
Investigation only.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Successful payments with no notification
Description:
*Business context*
Customers say they never got a receipt.

*Problem statement*
Some successful payments have no corresponding notification record at all, others are stuck unsent.

*Expected behaviour*
Quantify both groups, characterise them (channel, age, event type) and propose how the system should detect and repair each.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Counts for: never created, created-but-FAILED, created-but-PENDING
* Characterisation of each group
* Detection query that could run daily
* Notes any group that is expected/benign

*Scope*
Investigation only.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Bookings cancelled but the money was captured
Description:
*Business context*
Customers complain their cancelled bookings were not refunded.

*Problem statement*
Some cancelled bookings have a successful payment and no refund.

*Expected behaviour*
Find them, total the amount held, split by age, and explain the possible origins using code and data.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Complete list and total money held
* Distinguishes bookings cancelled by customer, by payment failure and by an operator
* Recommended remediation that cannot double-refund

*Scope*
Investigation only.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Subscriptions whose state does not match their payments
Description:
*Business context*
Finance found subscribers with access they did not pay for, and payers without access.

*Problem statement*
Some ACTIVE subscriptions have no successful payment; some PENDING ones have.

*Expected behaviour*
List both groups with amounts and dates, and check streaming access implications for each group.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Both groups quantified
* For three sample customers, shows whether play is allowed or denied and why
* Proposes the corrective action for each group

*Scope*
Investigation only; exercise the play endpoint as test customers if needed.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Why did this refund return 409 / 400?
Description:
*Business context*
A support agent pasted three failed refund calls from a customer and cannot explain the errors.

*Problem statement*
Refund attempts return different errors depending on the payment.

*Expected behaviour*
Reproduce each error class with real payments from the dataset and explain it in plain language, with the exact rule behind each.

*Acceptance criteria*
* At least four distinct error situations reproduced
* Each linked to the rule in code and a SQL check
* Correlation ids included

*Scope*
Investigation only; use dataset payments.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Reconciliation backlog report
Description:
*Business context*
Finance wants a weekly number.

*Problem statement*
No report exists for payments needing reconciliation.

*Expected behaviour*
A SQL report: count and amount by reconciliation_state, status, age bucket and payment type.

*Acceptance criteria*
* One query or small set of queries, parameter-free
* Verified against the admin dashboard figure
* Runs in under 1 second on the dataset

*Scope*
SQL deliverable only.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Which accounts are locked and why?
Description:
*Business context*
Customers phone in saying they cannot log in.

*Problem statement*
Some accounts are LOCKED, PENDING or DISABLED; support cannot tell which reason applies.

*Expected behaviour*
A lookup guide: for each account status, what it means, how it arises, how it ends, and a query that explains one customer's login state.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Covers every account status
* Shows the lockout window rule
* Includes a query using app_user and customer_profile
* States what support may and may not do

*Scope*
Read-only.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Reconstruct one customer's month
Description:
*Business context*
A customer disputes their month's charges.

*Problem statement*
There is no single view that lists their recharges, payments, refunds, coupons and notifications chronologically.

*Expected behaviour*
A single SQL query (UNION ALL of events) producing a chronological statement for any customer id and month, plus a worked example for customer 1.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Includes recharges, payments, refunds, coupon redemptions, bookings, subscriptions
* Totals reconcile to payments minus refunds
* Runs fast for the heaviest customer

*Scope*
SQL deliverable only.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Same phone number can register twice
Description:
*Business context*
Support found two accounts for one person; refunds went to the wrong account.

*Problem statement*
Registering with a phone number that differs from an existing one only by a leading '+' is accepted.

*Expected behaviour*
A number identifies exactly one customer regardless of how it was typed.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Registration with +9190... and 9190... of the same number is rejected with a clear 409/400
* Existing validation behaviour for other inputs is unchanged
* Add-mobile-number follows the same rule
* Failing test added first
* Explain what to do about duplicates already in the data

*Scope*
Identity + customer modules. Include data-impact analysis; do not mass-update data.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Expired subscription shows as ACTIVE as soon as a renewal is requested
Description:
*Business context*
Finance and the customer dashboard count 'active subscribers'; the numbers are inflated and customers are confused.

*Problem statement*
A customer with an expired subscription sees it as ACTIVE the moment they start a renewal, before any payment has succeeded. If they never pay, it stays labelled ACTIVE until a background job notices.

*Expected behaviour*
The subscription's status must reflect reality: it becomes ACTIVE only when the renewal payment succeeds, and an abandoned or failed renewal leaves it expired.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Reproduced with a failing test (status checked right after the renew call, then after confirm SUCCEEDED / FAILED / payment expiry)
* Status and entitlement never disagree at any point of the flow
* Existing renewal of a currently-active subscription is unchanged
* Subscription events describe what actually happened
* Report states how many existing rows could be in an inconsistent state and how you checked

*Scope*
Subscription + payment confirmation code. Do not repair existing data in this ticket.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: A coupon redeemed on its own can no longer be used at checkout
Description:
*Business context*
Customers say 'I used my coupon, then it was refused when I paid'.

*Problem statement*
There are two ways to redeem a coupon and they interfere.

*Expected behaviour*
Product decision needed and implemented consistently: a coupon is consumed exactly once, by a payment.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Write down the rule you choose and why
* Behaviour is consistent for both entry points
* Concurrency/limit guarantees preserved (existing tests still pass)
* Frontend/API docs updated if an endpoint changes

*Scope*
Admin/coupon + checkout. Backward-compatibility note required.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Booking refund after the event has started
Description:
*Business context*
Finance found full refunds paid for events that had already happened.

*Problem statement*
A confirmed booking can be cancelled and fully refunded after the schedule's start time.

*Expected behaviour*
Cancellation after the start time must not produce a refund; the customer is told clearly.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Failing test first
* Cancellation after start is rejected or recorded without refund (choose and justify)
* Cancellation before start unchanged
* The 20+ historical cases in the dataset are listed in your report

*Scope*
Booking service. No retroactive data change.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Ticket queue cannot show how many tickets match
Description:
*Business context*
Agents cannot tell if there are 20 or 2,000 open tickets.

*Problem statement*
The staff ticket search returns only the current page; callers cannot know the total or whether there is a next page.

*Expected behaviour*
The response lets a client render accurate pagination.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Total and page information returned
* Backward-compatible or versioned (state which)
* Frontend queue pager updated to use it
* Test with more than one page

*Scope*
Support controller/service + frontend Tickets screen.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Legacy payment monitor silently truncates results
Description:
*Business context*
An analyst exported 'all failed payments' and got exactly 200 rows.

*Problem statement*
GET /payments returns at most 200 rows without saying so.

*Expected behaviour*
Callers can retrieve complete results or are told the result is limited.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Choose: paging or explicit limit metadata
* Document in API_REFERENCE.md
* No change to authorization
* Test with >200 matching rows

*Scope*
Payment controller/service.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Failed notifications are retried at a fixed interval forever-ish
Description:
*Business context*
The SMS vendor throttled us after an outage.

*Problem statement*
Retries of failing notifications are attempted at a constant short interval.

*Expected behaviour*
Retries back off progressively and stop after a bounded number of attempts with a visible final state.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Backoff schedule documented
* Final state after the last attempt is distinguishable from 'will retry'
* Admin deliveries view shows next attempt time
* Unit/integration test of the schedule

*Scope*
Notification service + admin view.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Suspended customers can still pay and refund
Description:
*Business context*
A suspended account was seen completing a refund.

*Problem statement*
Some payment actions do not take the customer's account status into account while other flows do.

*Expected behaviour*
A consistent rule for what a non-ACTIVE customer can and cannot do, enforced everywhere money moves.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Inventory of every money-moving endpoint and its status check
* Consistent behaviour implemented with tests per endpoint
* Error is the standard 403 contract
* Existing flows for ACTIVE customers unchanged

*Scope*
Payment, recharge, booking, subscription services.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: How quickly does a disabled account lose access? (verify first)
Description:
*Business context*
Security review question after an agent was disabled mid-shift.

*Problem statement*
It is not documented how quickly a disabled or suspended user loses access, for customers and for support agents, or what that costs per request.

*Expected behaviour*
Prove the current behaviour with tests for customers and agents; only change code if you find a real gap, and document the cost of the current approach either way.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Written finding with evidence for customers and for agents
* If a gap exists: fix + test; if none: a regression test that locks the behaviour in
* States the maximum exposure window
* Quantifies the per-request cost of the mechanism that provides it

*Scope*
Identity/security configuration.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Customer search treats wildcard characters literally as wildcards
Description:
*Business context*
An agent searched for '%' and got every customer.

*Problem statement*
Special characters in the search text change what is matched.

*Expected behaviour*
Search text is matched literally.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Failing test with '%' and '_'
* Normal searches (name, e-mail fragment, phone) unchanged
* Case-insensitivity preserved

*Scope*
Customer repository.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Coupon codes differing only by letter case are distinct
Description:
*Business context*
Two coupons 'SAVE10' and 'save10' exist and confuse customers.

*Problem statement*
Coupon code uniqueness and lookup are case sensitive.

*Expected behaviour*
Codes are unique and matched ignoring case.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Creation rejects case-insensitive duplicates
* Lookup at checkout ignores case
* A migration handles any existing conflicts safely (describe)
* Tests for creation and checkout

*Scope*
Admin + coupon service + migration.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Offers can be created that have already ended
Description:
*Business context*
Marketing created an offer that was expired on arrival.

*Problem statement*
The admin API accepts offers whose end is in the past.

*Expected behaviour*
Reasonable validation with clear error messages.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Past end date rejected with 400
* Editing/activating rules explained
* Frontend form shows the message
* Tests

*Scope*
Admin DTO/service + frontend Offers form.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Refund approval workflow
Description:
*Business context*
Finance wants control: customers should request refunds, staff should approve them.

*Problem statement*
Customer refunds are processed instantly with no review.

*Expected behaviour*
A customer submits a refund request; an authorised staff member approves or rejects; money state changes only on approval.

*Acceptance criteria*
* New states and migration, backward compatible with existing refunds
* Customer sees status in the UI
* Staff screen to approve/reject with reason
* Audit events for every decision
* Concurrency-safe (two approvers)
* Docs and tests updated

*Scope*
Payments, admin, frontend, migration.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Server-side pagination for customer lists
Description:
*Business context*
Heavy customers have hundreds of payments and notifications; pages load slowly.

*Problem statement*
Several customer list endpoints return everything (or a fixed cap) and the UI paginates in the browser.

*Expected behaviour*
Consistent server-side paging with total counts for payments, notifications, bookings and tickets.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Stable response shape documented
* Old clients keep working during a transition (state how)
* Frontend updated
* Load-test comparison for customer 1

*Scope*
Four endpoints + frontend pages.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Daily revenue and refund report with CSV export
Description:
*Business context*
Finance reconciles daily and copies numbers by hand.

*Problem statement*
No report exists beyond the dashboard totals.

*Expected behaviour*
An admin report by day and payment type (gross, discounts, refunds, net) with CSV download.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Date-range parameters validated
* Numbers tie out to payments and refunds tables (include a test)
* CSV streams without loading everything in memory
* Admin-only

*Scope*
Admin API + frontend page.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Charge auto-renewing subscriptions
Description:
*Business context*
Customers who ticked auto-renew expect to be charged.

*Problem statement*
autoRenew is stored but nothing renews the subscription.

*Expected behaviour*
A scheduled process initiates renewal payments shortly before expiry through the payment provider, idempotently, with failures visible.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Idempotent per subscription and period
* Failed renewals move to the correct state and notify the customer
* Safe with two application instances
* Audit/metrics for attempts
* Documented schedule properties

*Scope*
Subscription service, provider port, jobs, tests.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Password reset
Description:
*Business context*
Customers who forget their password have no recovery path.

*Problem statement*
There is no way to reset a password.

*Expected behaviour*
Request a reset via the OTP provider, verify, set a new password; all sessions are revoked.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Does not reveal whether an e-mail exists
* Rate limited and attempt limited
* Old refresh/access tokens revoked
* Strong password rules reused
* No secrets in logs
* UI screens + tests

*Scope*
Identity module + frontend.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Booking cancellation policy
Description:
*Business context*
The business wants tiered refunds based on time to event.

*Problem statement*
Cancellation refunds are all-or-nothing.

*Expected behaviour*
Configurable tiers (e.g. 100% > 48h, 50% > 24h, 0% afterwards) applied on cancel, with the customer shown the amount before confirming.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Policy stored in the database and editable by admin
* Partial refund recorded correctly (payment stays consistent)
* UI previews the refund
* Edge cases (exactly at a boundary, time zones) tested

*Scope*
Booking, payments, admin, frontend, migration.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Support ticket SLAs
Description:
*Business context*
Managers want to see which tickets are about to breach their response target.

*Problem statement*
Tickets have no due time.

*Expected behaviour*
Each ticket gets a due time from its priority; overdue tickets are flagged and sortable.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Due-time rules documented
* Breach flag in queue and dashboard
* Pausing while WAITING (decide and document)
* Migration for existing tickets
* Tests

*Scope*
Support, admin dashboard, frontend queue.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Coupon eligibility rules
Description:
*Business context*
Marketing wants 'minimum order value' and 'only for recharges'.

*Problem statement*
Coupons apply to any payment of any size.

*Expected behaviour*
Optional minimum amount and allowed product types per coupon, enforced at checkout and previewed in validation.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Admin can set rules
* Checkout and /coupons/validate agree
* Clear error messages
* Existing coupons keep working

*Scope*
Promotions, admin UI, migration.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Customer receipts
Description:
*Business context*
Customers ask for proof of payment.

*Problem statement*
No receipt exists.

*Expected behaviour*
An endpoint and screen returning a receipt (what was bought, amounts, discount, refunds) for a succeeded payment owned by the customer.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Ownership enforced
* Correct for recharge, booking and subscription
* Handles partial refunds
* Printable layout in the UI

*Scope*
Payments API + frontend.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Bulk notification retry from the admin UI
Description:
*Business context*
After a vendor outage ops wants to retry only the affected messages.

*Problem statement*
The only retry action is a global 'retry now'.

*Expected behaviour*
Filter failed notifications and retry a selection, with a result summary.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Filter by channel, event type, date
* Selection limit enforced server-side
* Idempotent and audited
* UI feedback for partial failures

*Scope*
Notifications, admin, frontend.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Continue watching
Description:
*Business context*
Viewers want to resume where they left off.

*Problem statement*
Progress is stored but never offered back.

*Expected behaviour*
An endpoint and shelf in the UI listing partially watched titles with resume position.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Uses latest progress per title
* Excludes finished titles (define threshold)
* Respects current entitlement
* Tests

*Scope*
Streaming API + frontend.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Notification preferences
Description:
*Business context*
Customers want to opt out of SMS marketing but keep payment receipts.

*Problem statement*
All notifications are sent on all channels.

*Expected behaviour*
Per-channel preferences honoured when events are enqueued, except mandatory transactional messages.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Preferences stored and editable
* Mandatory events cannot be disabled (define list)
* Existing idempotency preserved
* UI on the profile page
* Migration with sensible defaults

*Scope*
Notifications, customer, frontend, migration.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Recharge history is slow for heavy customers
Description:
*Business context*
Customer 1 (445 recharges) complains the recharge screen lags; support sees it too.

*Problem statement*
GET /recharges/me takes about 200 ms at p50 and 600 ms at p95 with ten concurrent users, far above lighter endpoints.

*Expected behaviour*
Find out why and bring p95 under 100 ms without changing the response.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Evidence of the cause from the database (query plan, not guesses)
* Fix delivered as a Flyway migration and/or code change
* Before/after plan and load-test numbers
* No regression in write latency (state how you checked)

*Scope*
Recharge queries, migration.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Customer search degrades as customers grow
Description:
*Business context*
The agent console search feels slow and gets slower with data.

*Problem statement*
Searching customers by a name fragment takes over a second under modest load.

*Expected behaviour*
Responsive search at 10k customers and a clear plan for 1M.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Baseline measured (single and concurrent)
* Options compared (e.g. different matching strategies) with trade-offs
* Chosen approach implemented and measured
* Behaviour of existing queries preserved or changes documented

*Scope*
Customer search, migration, possibly frontend debounce.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Ticket lists slow down as the table grows
Description:
*Business context*
The customer 'my tickets' screen and agent queue slow down daily.

*Problem statement*
Per-customer ticket lookups and some queue filters read far more rows than they return.

*Expected behaviour*
Predictable, small, indexed access for the main ticket queries.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Identify every ticket query that scans
* Evidence with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before/after
* Migration reviewed for lock impact on a big table
* No new index without a measured benefit

*Scope*
Support queries, migration.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Notification analytics query is slow
Description:
*Business context*
A daily report counting notifications by event type takes about 100 ms and is growing.

*Problem statement*
Counting notifications by event type reads the whole table.

*Expected behaviour*
The report runs in a few milliseconds or is served differently.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Measured baseline
* Solution with trade-offs explained (index vs summary table vs other)
* Write-amplification considered
* Test or script to reproduce the measurement

*Scope*
Notifications, migration.

*Difficulty*: Easy

Summary: Admin dashboard takes almost a second
Description:
*Business context*
Admins open the dashboard many times a day and wait.

*Problem statement*
The dashboard endpoint is the slowest read in the system under load.

*Expected behaviour*
Dashboard in under 200 ms at p95 with correct figures.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Per-statement timing of the endpoint
* Fix without changing the numbers (tests prove equality)
* Considers caching and its staleness trade-off explicitly

*Scope*
Admin operations service.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Login throughput under concurrency
Description:
*Business context*
A marketing campaign will cause many simultaneous sign-ins.

*Problem statement*
Ten simultaneous logins take about 0.8 seconds at p50; other requests are slower while they run.

*Expected behaviour*
A capacity analysis and safe improvements without weakening password security.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Where the time goes, measured (CPU profile/thread dumps)
* Effect on unrelated endpoints quantified
* Proposed mitigations ranked by risk (what you will NOT do and why)
* At least one implemented with a before/after load test

*Scope*
Identity/security configuration, load test script.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Redis outage adds latency to every request
Description:
*Business context*
During a Redis outage the catalogue endpoint became noticeably slower though it kept working.

*Problem statement*
While Redis is unreachable each cached call still waits before falling back to the database.

*Expected behaviour*
A cache outage should cost almost nothing after it is detected, and recovery should be automatic.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Reproduce with docker stop/start and measure per-request latency
* Implement fail-fast behaviour with automatic recovery
* Test for outage and recovery
* Document operational behaviour in the playbook

*Scope*
Cache configuration, tests, docs.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Customers sometimes get a server error cancelling a booking as payment confirms
Description:
*Business context*
Support sees occasional 500s on booking cancellation that vanish when the customer retries.

*Problem statement*
When two operations touch the same booking at the same moment (for example the customer cancels while the payment callback arrives) one of them can fail with a server error.

*Expected behaviour*
Every interleaving of cancel, confirm, expiry and refund on one booking ends in a well-defined, consistent outcome with a meaningful response for the loser.

*Acceptance criteria*
* A race test for each pair of operations that reproduces the failure rate you observe
* Invariants asserted (payment and booking agree, at most one seat claim, no money lost)
* Failures are eliminated or converted into the standard 409 contract
* Report states the lock order each code path uses and the order you standardise on
* Same analysis for subscriptions and recharges

*Scope*
Booking, payments, jobs, tests.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Own Payments & Reconciliation
Description:
*Business context*
Reconciliation is manual and slow; finance wants it dependable.

*Problem statement*
Stuck payments rely on a person noticing them.

*Expected behaviour*
A design and delivery for automatic detection and resolution of stuck payments with reporting, safe by construction.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Design note with state machine, failure modes and idempotency story
* Automatic resolution for the safe cases; humans for the rest
* Reports and alerts
* Backward-compatible migrations and data repair plan for existing rows
* Regression + concurrency tests
* Runbook

*Scope*
Cross-layer: DB, API, jobs, admin UI, docs.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Own Booking
Description:
*Business context*
Bookings need holds, policies and reliable release of seats.

*Problem statement*
Seat release, cancellation rules and expiry behaviour are spread across services.

*Expected behaviour*
A coherent booking module: seat holds with expiry, cancellation policy, and a single place for seat lifecycle rules.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Design note including invariants
* Refactor without behaviour regressions (tests first)
* Hold expiry and release verified under concurrency
* UI shows hold countdown

*Scope*
Booking + payments interaction, UI, tests.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Own Subscriptions
Description:
*Business context*
Retention depends on graceful renewals.

*Problem statement*
Failures end in an abrupt state change with no retry or grace period.

*Expected behaviour*
Renewal with retry schedule (dunning), grace period for entitlement, and clear customer communication.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Design note (states, timers, entitlement during grace)
* Idempotent retries, multi-instance safe
* Notifications at each stage
* Metrics and admin visibility
* Migration for new states

*Scope*
Subscriptions, notifications, streaming entitlement, UI.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Own Notifications and decide the async architecture
Description:
*Business context*
More consumers of business events are coming (analytics, fraud).

*Problem statement*
Notifications use a database queue; the team debates introducing a message broker.

*Expected behaviour*
An evidence-based decision and the implementation of the chosen path.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Written architecture decision record comparing at least outbox vs broker with failure modes and operations cost
* Implementation with at-least-once delivery and duplicate protection
* Dead-letter view for operators
* Load test of the chosen approach
* Rollback plan

*Scope*
Notifications and event publishing, ops docs.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Incident drill: customers charged twice
Description:
*Business context*
You are on call: finance reports a wave of double charges.

*Problem statement*
A realistic incident with data already in the system.

*Expected behaviour*
Handle it end to end like a production incident: triage, mitigate, repair data safely, communicate, and write the postmortem.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Timeline with evidence and correlation ids
* Mitigation that stops new double charges
* Reviewed data-repair script that is idempotent and auditable
* Customer communication draft
* Postmortem with prevention tickets (and at least one regression test added)

*Scope*
Whole system. Dev database only; repair script must be dry-run capable.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Introduce API v2 for payments without breaking v1
Description:
*Business context*
Clients depend on today's payment responses but we need paging and richer fields.

*Problem statement*
There is no versioning strategy.

*Expected behaviour*
A versioned API with a deprecation plan, shared service logic and a migrated frontend.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Design note (URL vs header versioning, error contract)
* v1 behaviour frozen by tests
* v2 with paging, receipts and refund state
* Frontend moved to v2
* Deprecation/communication plan

*Scope*
Controllers, DTOs, frontend, docs.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Extract the support/ticketing module into its own service
Description:
*Business context*
Support runs on its own cadence and team; it should deploy and scale independently of payments.

*Problem statement*
Support tickets share a database, transactions and code with the rest of core-service. Releasing a ticket change means redeploying payments.

*Expected behaviour*
A support-service with its own database, API behind the gateway, and events for the integration points, delivered with no downtime for existing clients.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Design note: boundary, data ownership, which events cross it (follow docs/MICROSERVICES.md checklist)
* Own database + Flyway; scripted, re-runnable data migration
* Gateway route switch with the old path kept until verified
* Customer-id / agent-id references have no cross-database foreign keys; say how integrity is protected instead
* Contract tests on both sides; compose + CI updated
* Old code and legacy tables removed in a separate, later migration

*Scope*
New module, gateway, compose, CI, docs. Tickets assigned to agents need agent identity: decide how (claims vs lookup).

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Rate limiting at the gateway
Description:
*Business context*
A client bug and a bot both hammered login and recharge endpoints last week.

*Problem statement*
The gateway forwards every request without any limit.

*Expected behaviour*
Per-client (and per-user for authenticated calls) rate limits with correct 429 responses, configurable per route, observable in metrics.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Strict limit on /auth/** and a looser one on the rest
* 429 with Retry-After and the standard JSON error body incl. correlation id
* State store choice justified (in-memory vs Redis) and consequences for several gateway instances
* Test that proves the limit and that normal use is unaffected
* Metric for rejected requests

*Scope*
api-gateway, docs, tests.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Circuit breaker and timeouts between gateway and services
Description:
*Business context*
When notification-service is down the notifications screen hangs for several seconds before failing.

*Problem statement*
Calls to a dead or slow downstream service are retried by the browser and tie up gateway threads.

*Expected behaviour*
Fail fast with a clear response while a service is unhealthy, recover automatically, and keep unrelated routes unaffected.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Reproduce the slow failure (docker stop) and record the latency before/after
* Circuit breaker + fallback response designed per route (what should the UI see?)
* Thread/connection usage of the gateway measured during the outage
* Retry policy only on idempotent methods; explain why
* Documented in the playbook with the fault-injection steps

*Scope*
api-gateway, frontend error state.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Distributed tracing across gateway, core and notification-service
Description:
*Business context*
The correlation id helps with logs but nobody can see where time is spent across services.

*Problem statement*
There are no spans; latency in the event pipeline is invisible.

*Expected behaviour*
Traces covering HTTP hops and the Kafka hop, visible in a local trace UI, with the correlation id linked to the trace id.

*Acceptance criteria*
* OpenTelemetry/Micrometer tracing wired in all three services
* Trace context propagated through the Kafka record headers (producer and consumer)
* A local trace backend added to the observability compose profile
* Screenshot-level description of one recharge trace in your report
* Overhead measured

*Scope*
All services, compose, docs.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Saga: payment, booking and notification consistency
Description:
*Business context*
Once booking and payment live in different services a failure between them leaves money taken without a seat, or a seat without payment.

*Problem statement*
Today a single database transaction hides this problem; after extraction it becomes real.

*Expected behaviour*
A choreographed or orchestrated saga for 'book a seat and pay' with compensations for every failure point.

*Acceptance criteria*
* State machine for the saga incl. every failure and timeout
* Idempotent steps and idempotent compensations
* Failure injection tests (service down between steps, duplicate events, out-of-order events)
* Operator view of stuck sagas
* Decision record: choreography vs orchestration for this flow

*Scope*
Design first; implement across payment/booking modules and events.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Replace the shared JWT secret with asymmetric signing
Description:
*Business context*
Every service holding the signing secret can mint tokens, and a token revoked at logout stays valid on notification-service until it expires.

*Problem statement*
All services share one HS256 secret and the notification service cannot check revocation.

*Expected behaviour*
Only the identity side can sign; other services verify with public keys; revocation behaviour is explicit and tested.

*Acceptance criteria*
* RS256/EdDSA with a JWKS endpoint and key rotation story
* Verification library code shared or duplicated deliberately (justify)
* Maximum exposure window for a revoked token stated and tested; mitigation chosen (short expiry, introspection, deny-list)
* Rollout plan that does not log everyone out
* Update of the local, compose and Terraform configuration

*Scope*
core-service, notification-service, gateway, infra, docs.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Flaky Redis cache test in the full suite
Description:
*Business context*
A CI run failed once and passed on re-run; the team loses trust in red builds.

*Problem statement*
RedisCacheTests failed once inside the full multi-module run (a thread-pool shutdown error) but passes alone.

*Expected behaviour*
A deterministic test suite: either a root cause fix or a justified isolation.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Reproduce with repeated full runs and record the failure rate
* Root cause explained with evidence (not 'timing')
* Fix verified over at least 20 consecutive full runs
* No test is simply disabled

*Scope*
core-service tests / cache configuration.

*Difficulty*: Medium

Summary: Outbox relay at scale
Description:
*Business context*
The relay publishes one record at a time while holding a database transaction open.

*Problem statement*
Throughput is limited and a slow broker keeps transactions (and row locks) open for seconds.

*Expected behaviour*
A relay design that sustains 1,000 events/s and does not hold locks while waiting for Kafka.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Measure the current maximum events/s and lock hold time
* Alternative designs compared (batching, claim-then-publish, CDC) with failure modes
* Ordering per customer preserved or the change explained
* Chosen design implemented with a load test and outage test
* Backlog/lag metrics and an alert rule

*Scope*
core-service outbox, metrics, docs.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Run the platform on a local Kubernetes cluster
Description:
*Business context*
AWS runs this on ECS today, but most employers ask about Kubernetes.

*Problem statement*
There are no Kubernetes manifests.

*Expected behaviour*
kind/minikube manifests (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, probes, resource limits, an Ingress) that run the whole platform with rolling updates.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Use readiness/liveness probes backed by the existing actuator endpoints
* Resource requests/limits that fit the available memory
* A rolling update and a rollback demonstrated with kubectl
* Kustomize overlays for dev and staging
* A README with every command and what to observe

*Scope*
New k8s/ directory, docs.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Update the AWS Terraform and CD pipeline for three services
Description:
*Business context*
The Terraform and CD workflow still describe the single-backend topology that existed before extraction.

*Problem statement*
AWS would only run core-service; the gateway, the notification service, Kafka and its database are missing.

*Expected behaviour*
Infrastructure and pipeline that deploy all services: service-to-service discovery, a managed Kafka, per-service databases, per-service rollouts.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Service discovery approach chosen and justified (Cloud Map / Service Connect / ALB paths)
* Managed Kafka or an explicit alternative with cost estimate
* Second database created reproducibly (not by hand)
* CD builds and deploys each service independently and only when its code changed
* terraform plan is clean; secrets only via Secrets Manager
* Cost estimate and a destroy procedure documented

*Scope*
infra/terraform, .github/workflows, docs/DEVOPS_AWS.md.

*Difficulty*: Hard

Summary: Blue/green deployment rehearsal for core-service
Description:
*Business context*
The local deploy script rolls in place; production teams often shift traffic between two versions.

*Problem statement*
There is no way to run two versions of core-service side by side and switch traffic.

*Expected behaviour*
A local blue/green procedure with an instant, verified switch and instant rollback.

*Acceptance criteria*
* Two versions running in Compose with different tags
* Traffic switch at the gateway (config or route weights) without downtime
* Database migration compatibility rules written down (expand/contract)
* Smoke test gates the switch; rollback demonstrated

*Scope*
compose, gateway, scripts/deploy-local.ps1, docs.

*Difficulty*: Medium
